names.name: The donut on the roof
names.said: Twenty-two feet of plaster ring, and it still works.

text.what: Oversize donuts built on or around Southern California shops to catch drivers: roadside novelty architecture, most of it from the decade after the Second World War.
text.story:
Randy's, beside the 405 near LAX, is the best known of four surviving big donuts built by Russell C. Wendell, who started the Big Do-Nut Drive-In chain in the 1940s. A fifth was converted into a bagel. At one point there were ten Do-Nut Drive-Ins with 22-foot rings — or thirty feet high, depending on the account. The first opened in December 1949 with clowns, jugglers, magicians, free coffee and a trapeze artist swinging from the middle of the hole.

Mrs. Chapman's Angel Food Donuts ran about twenty stores with slightly smaller rings. The Donut Hole in La Puente, a drive-through you enter and leave through the holes of two giant donuts, is described as a distant cousin of the rooftop kind.

One critic called the giant donuts part of a Los Angeles that "bordered on pop art, celebrating the effusiveness of life in the years after World War II" — the same city that gave America an orange juice stand shaped like an orange.
text.today: Municipal construction codes now generally prohibit oversize object-shaped buildings, so the survivors cannot be replaced, only kept.
